title: The Value of Waiting
topic: Queues, rationing and what economists call the price of time
passage:
A queue is a curious institution. It allocates something scarce without money changing hands, and it does so according to a rule most people accept without argument: those who arrive first are served first. Economists have long been uneasy about this arrangement, because a queue does not eliminate cost so much as relocate it. What the customer saves in cash is paid in time, and time, unlike money, cannot be transferred to the seller. It is simply destroyed. From the point of view of total welfare, a queue is a peculiar mechanism in which the resource used to ration demand vanishes rather than accruing to anyone.

This observation has an uncomfortable corollary. If a shortage is met by raising the price, the seller captures the difference and may reinvest it in supply. If the same shortage is met by a queue, nobody captures anything, and the shortage persists. The conclusion drawn by a certain school of thought is that queues represent waste, and that a market clearing at a higher price would leave society better off. The argument is internally consistent, and it is also incomplete, for reasons that become apparent when one asks who stands in queues and why.

The defence of the queue rests on distribution. Willingness to pay is not the same as intensity of need. A wealthy person may pay a high price for a ticket they value only mildly, while a poorer person who values it intensely is excluded. Waiting, by contrast, is a currency in which most people hold roughly comparable reserves: an hour costs an hour, whoever spends it. On this reading, queues are not a failure of allocation but a deliberate, if inefficient, choice to allocate by intensity of desire rather than by capacity to pay. It is a defence with an obvious weakness — the value of an hour varies enormously between a retired person and a parent working two jobs — but it captures something the pure efficiency argument misses.

The matter is complicated further by the fact that queues are rarely the passive phenomena the theory imagines. Where waiting has value, markets emerge to trade it. Professional queuers have operated outside courtrooms and legislative hearings, holding places for lobbyists who arrive shortly before proceedings begin. Ticket resale performs the same function at one remove, converting the willingness to wait of one person into the willingness to pay of another. Each of these developments quietly reintroduces the price mechanism the queue was meant to displace, which suggests that the choice between waiting and paying is less clean than it first appears.

Queues also carry information, and organisations have learned to exploit it. A line outside a restaurant is read by passers-by as evidence of quality, and some establishments seat customers more slowly than they could in order to maintain the impression. The signal is only reliable if it is costly to fake, and it is not: a queue can be manufactured. Yet the practice persists because the inference is intuitive, and because most observers do not stop to ask whether the delay they are witnessing is an accident of demand or a deliberate piece of theatre.

Behavioural research has added a further layer, showing that the experience of waiting is only loosely related to its duration. Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. Uncertain waits feel longer than waits of known length, which is why an accurate estimate of remaining delay improves satisfaction even when it lengthens the wait. Unexplained waits are the most irritating of all, and unfair ones — being overtaken by a later arrival — provoke a response out of all proportion to the seconds lost. Organisations that grasp this can improve the perception of a service without adding a single unit of capacity, which is either an efficiency or a sleight of hand depending on one's view.

What emerges is that the queue is not a primitive arrangement awaiting replacement by a properly functioning market. It is a distinct allocation system with its own logic, its own inefficiencies and its own quiet politics. Societies choose queues for some goods and prices for others, and the choices are not arbitrary: emergency medicine is rationed by urgency, concert tickets increasingly by price, elections strictly by arrival. Each rule expresses a judgement about what the good is for. The economist's discomfort with waiting is well founded as far as it goes, but it measures only one of the things a queue is doing.

questions.statement: The time spent queuing is transferred to the seller as a form of payment.
questions.explanation: The passage says time "cannot be transferred to the seller. It is simply destroyed." The statement claims a transfer takes place, so FALSE.

questions.statement: The writer regards the efficiency argument against queues as logically sound but partial.
questions.explanation: "The argument is internally consistent, and it is also incomplete" — sound as far as it goes, but partial. TRUE.

questions.statement: Professional queuers earn more than the lobbyists who employ them.
questions.explanation: Professional queuers are described, but nothing is said about what they earn compared with the lobbyists. NOT GIVEN.

questions.statement: A queue outside a business is difficult to create artificially.
questions.explanation: "The signal is only reliable if it is costly to fake, and it is not: a queue can be manufactured." So creating one artificially is easy, and the statement is FALSE.

questions.statement: Telling people how long they must wait can improve their satisfaction.
questions.explanation: "An accurate estimate of remaining delay improves satisfaction even when it lengthens the wait." TRUE.

questions.question: What does the writer identify as the central peculiarity of rationing by queue?
options: The resource used to ration demand is destroyed
questions.explanation: "A queue is a peculiar mechanism in which the resource used to ration demand vanishes rather than accruing to anyone." That destruction is the peculiarity the writer identifies.

questions.question: The main weakness the writer concedes in the distributional defence of queues is that
options: an hour is not equally costly to everyone
questions.explanation: The writer names the weakness directly: "the value of an hour varies enormously between a retired person and a parent working two jobs".

questions.question: What do professional queuing and ticket resale have in common, according to the passage?
options: They both bring price back into the allocation
They both rely on new technology
questions.explanation: "Each of these developments quietly reintroduces the price mechanism the queue was meant to displace."

questions.question: The writer's overall position is that queues are
options: an inefficient system that markets should replace
a separate allocation system reflecting judgements about the good
questions.explanation: The final paragraph calls the queue "a distinct allocation system with its own logic" and says "each rule expresses a judgement about what the good is for".

questions.sentence: Some restaurants seat customers slowly to preserve the impression of ___.
questions.explanation: "A line outside a restaurant is read by passers-by as evidence of quality, and some establishments seat customers more slowly ... to maintain the impression."

questions.sentence: Research finds that ___ time feels shorter than time spent doing nothing.
questions.explanation: "Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time." The gap needs the adjective exactly as written.

questions.sentence: Being overtaken by someone who arrived later makes a wait feel ___.
questions.explanation: "Unfair ones — being overtaken by a later arrival — provoke a response out of all proportion." The gap needs the adjective "unfair".

questions.sentence: The writer notes that elections are rationed strictly by ___.
questions.explanation: "Elections strictly by arrival" — the last sentence of the list in the final paragraph.
